prompt:
Let $x_i, y_i$ $(i=1,2,\ldots,n)$ be real numbers such that
$$x_1\ge x_2\ge\cdots\ge x_n\quad\text{and}\quad y_1\ge y_2\ge\cdots\ge y_n.$$
Prove that, if $z_1,z_2,\ldots,z_n$ is any permutation of $y_1,y_2,\ldots,y_n$, then
$$\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-y_i)^2\le\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-z_i)^2.$$
answer: Proof: since $\sum y_i^2=\sum z_i^2$, it is equivalent to $\sum x_iy_i\ge\sum x_iz_i$ (rearrangement inequality), proved by swapping out-of-order pairs, each swap not decreasing $\sum x_iz_i$.

solutions.title: Reduce to $\sum x_iz_i\le\sum x_iy_i$ and sort by swaps
solutions.body:
Expanding the squares and using $\sum z_i^2=\sum y_i^2$ (the $z$'s are a permutation of the $y$'s), the inequality is equivalent to
$$\sum_{i=1}^n x_iz_i\le\sum_{i=1}^n x_iy_i. \tag{$*$}$$

**Swapping step.** If the sequence $z_1,\ldots,z_n$ is not non-increasing, there is an index $i$ with $z_i<z_{i+1}$. Exchange $z_i$ and $z_{i+1}$. The sum $\sum x_kz_k$ changes by
$$(x_iz_{i+1}+x_{i+1}z_i)-(x_iz_i+x_{i+1}z_{i+1})=(x_i-x_{i+1})(z_{i+1}-z_i)\ge0,$$
because $x_i\ge x_{i+1}$ and $z_{i+1}>z_i$. So the sum does not decrease.

**Termination.** Such an adjacent swap reduces the number of *inversions* (pairs $k<l$ with $z_k<z_l$) by exactly one. So after finitely many swaps the sequence is non-increasing, i.e. it is exactly $y_1\ge\cdots\ge y_n$ (the unique non-increasing arrangement of these numbers).

Since $\sum x_kz_k$ never decreased along the way, $\sum x_iz_i\le\sum x_iy_i$, which is $(*)$. ∎

prompt:
Let $a_1,a_2,a_3,\ldots$ be an infinite increasing sequence of positive integers. Prove that for every $p\ge1$ there are infinitely many $a_m$ which can be written in the form
$$a_m=xa_p+ya_q$$
with $x,y$ positive integers and $q>p$.
answer: Proof: infinitely many terms after $a_p$ share a residue mod $a_p$; if $a_q$ is the first of them, every later one is $a_m=a_q+xa_p$ with $x\ge1$ (take $y=1$).

solutions.title: Pigeonhole on residues modulo $a_p$
solutions.body:
Fix $p$. The infinitely many terms $a_{p+1},a_{p+2},\ldots$ have only $a_p$ possible remainders modulo $a_p$, so some remainder $\rho$ occurs for infinitely many of them. Let $q>p$ be the smallest index with $a_q\equiv\rho\pmod{a_p}$.

For every $m>q$ with $a_m\equiv\rho\pmod{a_p}$ (there are infinitely many such $m$), $a_m-a_q$ is divisible by $a_p$, and $a_m>a_q$ because the sequence is increasing. So
$$x=\frac{a_m-a_q}{a_p}$$
is a positive integer and
$$a_m=x\,a_p+1\cdot a_q ,$$
which is the required form with $y=1$ and $q>p$. This gives infinitely many such $a_m$. ∎

prompt: On the sides of an arbitrary triangle $ABC$, triangles $ABR$, $BCP$, $CAQ$ are constructed externally with $\angle CBP=\angle CAQ=45^\circ$, $\angle BCP=\angle ACQ=30^\circ$, $\angle ABR=\angle BAR=15^\circ$. Prove that $\angle QRP=90^\circ$ and $QR=RP$.
answer: Proof: in complex numbers with $A=0$, $P,Q,R$ are explicit linear expressions in $B,C$ (rotations by $\mp45^\circ$, $-15^\circ$ scaled by $\frac{1}{2\cos15^\circ}$), and one checks $Q-R=i\,(P-R)$.

solutions.title: Complex numbers
solutions.body:
We may assume $A,B,C$ are in counterclockwise order (otherwise reflect the figure; the claims are invariant). Use complex numbers with $A=0$, and write $e(\varphi)=\cos\varphi+i\sin\varphi$.

**Side lengths.** In triangle $BCP$ the angles are $45^\circ$ at $B$, $30^\circ$ at $C$, $105^\circ$ at $P$, so by the law of sines
$$BP=\frac{\sin30^\circ}{\sin105^\circ}\,BC=\rho\, BC,\qquad \rho=\frac{1}{2\sin105^\circ}=\frac{1}{2\cos15^\circ}.$$
Similarly in $CAQ$ (angles $45^\circ$ at $A$, $30^\circ$ at $C$): $AQ=\rho\,AC$. In the isosceles triangle $ABR$ (base angles $15^\circ$): $AR=\frac{AB}{2\cos15^\circ}=\rho\,AB$.

**Positions.** With $ABC$ counterclockwise, the interior lies to the left of $\vec{AB}$ and of $\vec{BC}$, and to the right of $\vec{AC}$. The triangles are external, so
$$P=B+\rho\,e(-45^\circ)(C-B),\qquad Q=\rho\,e(45^\circ)\,C,\qquad R=\rho\,e(-15^\circ)\,B .$$

**Check $Q-R=i(P-R)$.** We have
$$P-R=\big(1-\rho\,e(-45^\circ)-\rho\,e(-15^\circ)\big)B+\rho\,e(-45^\circ)C,\qquad Q-R=\rho\,e(45^\circ)C-\rho\,e(-15^\circ)B.$$
* Coefficient of $C$: $i\cdot\rho\,e(-45^\circ)=\rho\,e(45^\circ)$. ✓
* Coefficient of $B$: we need $-\rho\,e(-15^\circ)=i-\rho\,i\,e(-45^\circ)-\rho\,i\,e(-15^\circ)$, i.e.
$$\rho\big(e(45^\circ)+e(75^\circ)-e(-15^\circ)\big)=i,$$
using $i\,e(-45^\circ)=e(45^\circ)$ and $i\,e(-15^\circ)=e(75^\circ)$. Now
$$e(75^\circ)-e(-15^\circ)=(\cos75^\circ-\cos15^\circ)+i(\sin75^\circ+\sin15^\circ)=-\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}+i\,\tfrac{\sqrt6}{2},$$
(sum-to-product: $\cos75^\circ-\cos15^\circ=-2\sin45^\circ\sin30^\circ$, $\sin75^\circ+\sin15^\circ=2\sin45^\circ\cos30^\circ$), and $e(45^\circ)=\frac{\sqrt2}2+i\frac{\sqrt2}2$. The sum is $i\,\frac{\sqrt6+\sqrt2}{2}$, and since $\cos15^\circ=\frac{\sqrt6+\sqrt2}{4}$ we get $\rho\cdot i\,\frac{\sqrt6+\sqrt2}{2}=i$. ✓

Hence $Q-R=i(P-R)$: the vector $\vec{RQ}$ is $\vec{RP}$ rotated by $90^\circ$. Therefore $RQ=RP$ and $\angle QRP=90^\circ$. ∎

prompt: When $4444^{4444}$ is written in decimal notation, the sum of its digits is $A$. Let $B$ be the sum of the digits of $A$. Find the sum of the digits of $B$. ($A$ and $B$ are written in decimal notation.)

solutions.title: Size bounds plus casting out nines
solutions.body:
Let $N=4444^{4444}$ and let $s(\cdot)$ denote the digit sum. We want $s(B)$ where $A=s(N)$, $B=s(A)$.

**Size.** $N<10000^{4444}=10^{17776}$, so $N$ has at most $17776$ digits and $A\le 9\cdot17776=159984$. A number below $200000$ has digit sum at most $1+5\cdot9=46$, so $B\le46$. A number at most $46$ has digit sum at most $3+9=12$ (attained at $39$), so $s(B)\le12$.

**Residue mod 9.** A number and its digit sum are congruent modulo $9$, so $s(B)\equiv B\equiv A\equiv N\pmod 9$. Now $4444\equiv4+4+4+4=16\equiv7\pmod9$, and $7^3=343=38\cdot9+1\equiv1\pmod9$. Since $4444=3\cdot1481+1$,
$$N\equiv7^{4444}=(7^3)^{1481}\cdot7\equiv7\pmod9 .$$

So $s(B)$ is a positive integer at most $12$ that is $\equiv7\pmod9$, hence $s(B)=7$.

**Answer: $7$.**

prompt: Determine, with proof, whether or not one can find $1975$ points on the circumference of a circle with unit radius such that the distance between any two of them is a rational number.

solutions.title: Points at angles $2k\theta$ with $\cos\theta=\frac45$
solutions.body:
**Yes.** Let $\theta$ be the angle with $\cos\theta=\frac45$, $\sin\theta=\frac35$, and put $P_k=(\cos 2k\theta,\ \sin2k\theta)$ for $k=1,2,\ldots,1975$, all on the unit circle.

**Distances are rational.** By the chord-length formula, $|P_jP_k|=2\,|\sin((j-k)\theta)|$. Write $(4+3i)^m=a_m+b_mi$; then $a_m,b_m$ are integers and, since $\cos\theta+i\sin\theta=\frac{4+3i}{5}$, de Moivre gives
$$\cos m\theta=\frac{a_m}{5^m},\qquad \sin m\theta=\frac{b_m}{5^m},$$
both rational. So all distances are rational.

**The points are distinct.** $P_j=P_k$ ($j\ne k$) would mean $2(j-k)\theta$ is a multiple of $2\pi$, i.e. $\sin((j-k)\theta)=0$. We show $b_m\ne0$ for every $m\ge1$, in fact $b_m\not\equiv0\pmod5$. Modulo $5$,
$$(4+3i)^2=7+24i\equiv2+4i=3(4+3i)-10-5i\equiv 3(4+3i)\pmod 5,$$
(meaning real and imaginary parts are congruent mod $5$). By induction $(4+3i)^m\equiv3^{m-1}(4+3i)\pmod5$, so $b_m\equiv3^{m-1}\cdot3=3^m\not\equiv0\pmod 5$. Hence $\sin m\theta\ne0$ for all $m\ge1$ and the $1975$ points are distinct.

(The same construction gives arbitrarily many — even infinitely many — such points.)

**Answer: Yes.** ∎

prompt:
Find all polynomials $P$, in two variables, with the following properties:

(i) for a positive integer $n$ and all real $t,x,y$,
$$P(tx,ty)=t^nP(x,y)$$
(that is, $P$ is homogeneous of degree $n$),

(ii) for all real $a,b,c$,
$$P(b+c,a)+P(c+a,b)+P(a+b,c)=0,$$

(iii) $P(1,0)=1$.

solutions.title: Restrict to the line $x+y=1$
solutions.body:
**The polynomial works.** For $P(x,y)=(x-2y)(x+y)^{n-1}$: it is homogeneous of degree $n$, $P(1,0)=1$, and with $s=a+b+c$,
$$P(b+c,a)+P(c+a,b)+P(a+b,c)=s^{n-1}\big[(b+c-2a)+(c+a-2b)+(a+b-2c)\big]=0.$$

**It is the only one.** Let $P$ satisfy (i)–(iii) and define the one-variable polynomial $g(t)=P(1-t,t)$. If $a+b+c=1$, then $b+c=1-a$ etc., so (ii) says
$$g(a)+g(b)+g(c)=0\qquad\text{whenever }a+b+c=1. \tag{1}$$
* $a=b=c=\frac13$: $g(\frac13)=0$.
* $c=\frac13$: $g(a)+g(\frac23-a)=0$ for all $a$.
* Hence for $c=1-a-b$: $g(c)=-g(\frac23-c)=-g(a+b-\frac13)$, and (1) becomes $g(a)+g(b)=g(a+b-\frac13)$.

Put $h(x)=g(x+\frac13)$. With $a=x+\frac13$, $b=y+\frac13$ this reads $h(x)+h(y)=h(x+y)$ for all real $x,y$. Then $h(0)=0$ and $h(2x)=2h(x)$; writing $h(x)=\sum_j c_jx^j$, comparing coefficients gives $c_j2^j=2c_j$, so only $c_1$ can be nonzero: $h(x)=kx$. Thus $g(t)=k(t-\frac13)$, and $g(0)=P(1,0)=1$ gives $k=-3$:
$$P(1-t,t)=1-3t\quad\text{for all real }t.$$

Now take $(x,y)$ with $x+y\ne0$ and apply (i) with $t=x+y$ to the point $\big(\frac{x}{x+y},\frac{y}{x+y}\big)$, which lies on the line $u+v=1$:
$$P(x,y)=(x+y)^n\,P\Big(1-\tfrac{y}{x+y},\tfrac{y}{x+y}\Big)=(x+y)^n\Big(1-\tfrac{3y}{x+y}\Big)=(x+y)^{n-1}(x-2y).$$
Two polynomials that agree on the set $\{x+y\ne0\}$ (which is dense in the plane) agree everywhere, so $P(x,y)=(x-2y)(x+y)^{n-1}$.

**Answer: $P(x,y)=(x-2y)(x+y)^{n-1}$.** ∎
